sections.history: Thiruvottiyur, on the old coast north of Chennai, is among the most venerable shrines of the Thondai country. It is the Tiruvottiyur of the Tevaram, where Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar all sang, and the poet-saint Pattinathar is also remembered here, which makes it unusually rich in devotional memory. Counted as a Paadal Petra Sthalam, the temple is attributed to Pallava and Chola patronage, and the stone shrine has been enlarged over many centuries. The name Adipureeswarar means the Lord of the first city; tradition holds that the self-formed lingam here was the first to appear on the earth after the great dissolution. The deity is worshipped under several names, among them Adipureeswarar, Padampakkanathar and, in his festival form, Thyagaraja, which is why the temple is known in the city by more than one name.
sections.architecture: The temple is a Dravidian complex of the Pallava and Chola tradition, with later additions, set with two sacred tanks, the Brahma Theertham and the Adisesha Theertham. The sanctum holds the Adipureeswarar lingam, which is a self-formed mound, an anthill form that is kept covered with a protective armour and is revealed only on a few days of the year. The goddess Vadivudai Amman, regarded as the form of Tripurasundari, has her own shrine and is honoured as the power of wisdom, counted among the three great goddess shrines of Chennai. The Thyagaraja shrine houses the festival image of the Lord in a dancing form, known here as Ananda Thyagesar. A mandapam and a magizha tree mark the place of Sundarar's wedding, and a separate shrine to Vattaparai Amman stands within the precincts.
sections.legends: The best-loved story of Thiruvottiyur is Sundarar's. Having already married Paravai Nachiyar at Tiruvarur, the saint came here and fell in love with Sangili Nachiyar, a young woman of the town. Fearing that he would be taken from her, Sangili asked him to swear that he would never leave her, and Sundarar agreed. He asked the Lord himself to step out of the sanctum and stand beneath the magizha tree, so that the vow would be made before him; tradition says Shiva hid behind the tree, so that the promise was in truth given to the Lord and not to Sangili. When Sundarar later left Thiruvottiyur for Tiruvarur, the broken vow cost him his sight, which was restored only at later shrines on his journey. The wedding is kept alive as the Makizhadi Sevai, held on the ninth day of the temple's great festival. The lingam's own story is older: it is the first self-formed lingam, the Adi lingam, whose armour is removed on the full-moon night of Karthigai so that devotees may see the Lord in his natural anthill form.
sections.festivals: The great festival is the Masi Brahmotsavam, held over about ten days in February or March, when the Thyagaraja image goes out in procession in the early hours before dawn and is back in the temple before six in the morning. On its ninth day the wedding of Sundarar and Sangili Nachiyar is recalled beneath the magizha tree as the Makizhadi Sevai, and on the new-moon day of Makam the Lord is carried in a Nandi Nadanam on the western street. On the full moon of Karthigai the armour of Adipureeswarar is removed for three days of worship. The Vattaparai Amman festival is celebrated in the month of Chithirai. Maha Shivaratri, Navaratri, Thai Poosam, Aadi Pooram, Skanda Shashti and Arudra darshan are all observed, and Pradosham and the full moon days are kept with devotion. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Thiruvottiyur is a city temple with the weight of centuries, and it rewards an early visit. Enter beneath the gateway and walk the long corridors toward the sanctum of Adipureeswarar, where the covered mound of the first lingam is worshipped. Then turn to Vadivudai Amman, a shrine much loved by local families, and to the Thyagaraja shrine, where the Lord is honoured in his dancing form. Many pilgrims pause at the magizha tree and the wedding mandapam to recall Sundarar's vow, and the two temple tanks recall the older, wider setting of the shrine near the coast. The surrounding streets are busy, but within the walls the pace slows to that of worship.

visit.timings: Daily worship is reported from early morning, with services at around 6 am, 8 am and noon, and again in the evening around 6 pm; opening and closing hours are not confirmed, so check locally, especially on festival days when timings change.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands on Thiruvottiyur High Road in north Chennai, near the Therady bus stop. Thiruvottiyur is served by city buses and by Chennai's suburban railway line, and the temple is a short auto ride from the station. Chennai International Airport lies across the city to the south, and a taxi or app cab from the airport or from central Chennai is the simplest approach.
